newsitem.title: USA: Japanese transport official opposes "open skies".
newsitem.headline: Japanese transport official opposes "open skies".

text.p: U.S. airlines would dominate the Japanese airline market if the United States and Japan adopted a more liberal "open skies" air treaty, said Jiro Hanyu, the deputy director general of the Japan Ministry of Transport.

"What would happen if U.S. airlines rushed into a market ... like Japan? It is clear that U.S. airlines can dominate the market," said Hanyu, speaking at the Sixth Annual Phoenix International Aviation Symposium.

Hanyu cited competition trends within the U.S. since airline deregulation in the late 1970s. Hanyu said as competition increased, some carriers went out of business, while the airlines that survived gained market dominance and culled "huge profits."

If those same carriers were allowed to enter the Japanese market under an open skies treaty similar to those formed between the U.S. and some European countries, Japanese airlines would suffer, Hanyu said.
"Market concentration become higher when unrestricted competition is allowed," he said.

The U.S. and Japan have been in talks to develop a more liberal aviation treaty, but no agreement has been reached. Currently, only UAL Corp's United Airlines and Northwest Airlines have full access to the Japanese market. Other carriers, such as AMR Corp's American Airlines and Delta Air Lines Inc, operate on a restricted basis.
Charles Hunnicutt, assistant secretary for aviation and international affairs for the U.S. Department of Transportation, said "liberalization is an idea whose time has come."
"More and more nations understand that everyone benefits from aviation liberalization," Hunnicutt said.
Open skies treaties have opened new markets, increased trade opportunities and expanded consumer travel options, Hunnicutt said.
Hanyu said he supports liberalization "in principle," but cautioned that "we should realize that all policies have a bright side and a dark side."
"It's not that I hate open skies, but (it's) that I love fair competition," Hanyu said.
Hanyu said other obstacles in a new open skies treaty include air fare pricing policies and slot rights at airports.
